baseline: Host Linux 6.8.0-124-generic, pinned LTP 20260529 prebuilt (/nix/store/hik6kb512ia3p14lc2vwzb292d4k306a-ltp-20260529/testcases/bin/prctl05): passed 8, failed 0. Two tcases, 4 assertions each. tcase 1 setname='prctl05_test' (12 bytes): PR_SET_NAME returns 0; PR_GET_NAME yields 'prctl05_test'; /proc/self/task/<tid>/comm and /proc/self/comm both read 'prctl05_test'. tcase 2 setname='prctl05_test_xxxxx' (18 bytes, i.e. 19 including nul): PR_SET_NAME still returns 0 -- the over-long name is SILENTLY TRUNCATED, not rejected; PR_GET_NAME then yields 'prctl05_test_xx' (15 bytes) and both comm files read 'prctl05_test_xx'. Per assertion, the correct kernel therefore returns: prctl(PR_SET_NAME, <any readable string>) = 0 regardless of length, and the stored name = first min(len, TASK_COMM_LEN-1 = 15) bytes. The 15-byte cut is what the test hard-codes as expname, so truncation-to-15 is the specified behaviour, not an implementation detail.
failing_assertion: prctl05.c:45: TFAIL: prctl(PR_SET_NAME) failed: ENAMETOOLONG (36) -- captured verbatim from qemu.log line 56 on the second boot, run with KIRK_VERBOSE=1 to make kirk emit per-case lines. Asterinas returns -1/ENAMETOOLONG for tcase 2's 18-byte name where the correct value is 0 with the name truncated to 'prctl05_test_xx'. Test totals: Passed 4 / Failed 1 / Broken 0 / Skipped 0 vs host 8/0/0/0. The 4-not-5 pass count is itself confirmation of the shape: tcase 2 fails at the very first check and takes the `return` at prctl05.c:46, so its remaining three assertions (lines 48, 62, 67-68) never execute. tcase 1 passes all four assertions, so PR_GET_NAME, /proc/self/comm and /proc/self/task/<tid>/comm are all already correct -- the whole divergence is the one error return.
root_cause: sys_prctl's PR_SET_NAME arm (kernel/src/syscall/prctl.rs:65-71) marshals the name with `ctx.user_space().read_cstring(read_addr, MAX_THREAD_NAME_LEN)?` -- the reject-on-overflow reader, where this syscall needs a truncate-on-overflow one. MAX_THREAD_NAME_LEN is 16 (kernel/src/process/posix_thread/name.rs:5). CurrentUserSpace::read_cstring (kernel/src/context.rs:202-228) delegates to VmReader::read_cstring_until_nul (kernel/src/util/read_cstring.rs:42-55), whose helper read_until_nul_byte (same file, 105-153) stops once `buffer.len() < max_len` goes false and returns Ok(false) when it never saw a nul byte. read_cstring turns that None into an error at context.rs:214-227, and picks ENAMETOOLONG over EFAULT on the branch `userspace_max_len == max_len`; tcases[] is a static array in the test image, nowhere near VMAR_CAP_ADDR, so userspace_max_len == max_len == 16 and the ENAMETOOLONG arm is the one taken -- matching the observed errno exactly. 'prctl05_test_xxxxx' is 18 non-nul bytes, so no nul appears in the first 16 and the `?` at prctl.rs:68 propagates ENAMETOOLONG out of the syscall before any thread state is touched. The boundary is name length >= 16: at exactly 15 bytes the nul is the 16th byte read and the call still succeeds. Note the truncation logic itself is already correct and already present one layer down -- ThreadName::set_name_as_bytes (name.rs:29-33) clamps to MAX_THREAD_NAME_LEN-1 = 15 and zero-fills the rest -- so the stored name would have come out right; line 68 simply errors out before line 70 can ever hand it the bytes. read_cstring is not itself at fault: its own doc comment at context.rs:199-201 says it is for file names and paths, that ENAMETOOLONG is the correct code in that case, and that 'in other cases, the caller may want to fix the error code manually'. This caller is one of those other cases and does not.
invariant: Setting a thread name from user space is a truncating operation, never a length-validating one: a name longer than the kernel's fixed comm field (TASK_COMM_LEN = 16 bytes including the terminating nul) is silently cut to the first 15 bytes and the operation reports success. The only failure mode is an unreadable source address (EFAULT); an over-long but readable name is never an error. Corollary, and the part that is easy to get wrong: the fixed-size thread-name field is the single place that decides where the cut falls, so every path that sets a name must route through it rather than clamping on its own.
owning_layer: The syscall-entry argument-marshalling layer -- specifically the PR_SET_NAME arm of sys_prctl in kernel/src/syscall/prctl.rs:65-71, which must choose a truncating user-space string reader. Truncation enforcement stays where it already is, in ThreadName::set_name_as_bytes (kernel/src/process/posix_thread/name.rs:29-33); that function is correct and must not be touched. This is a two-level split and both levels matter: the entry decides that over-length is legal, the ThreadName field decides where the cut lands. Explicitly NOT the layer to fix: CurrentUserSpace::read_cstring / read_cstring_until_nul. Its ENAMETOOLONG is right for the other 51 of 52 call sites (paths under MAX_FILENAME_LEN / PATH_MAX, plus memfd_create and xattr names), and changing it there would silently break every one of them. Asterinas's abstractions line up with Linux's here, so no design divergence needs recording.
linux_reference: Linux enforces the same rule at the same two levels. In the syscall entry, SYSCALL_DEFINE5(prctl, ...) in kernel/sys.c pre-zeroes the last byte of a local comm[TASK_COMM_LEN] and then calls strncpy_from_user(comm, (char __user *)arg2, sizeof(me->comm) - 1), i.e. count = 15, treating only a negative return (a fault) as -EFAULT; strncpy_from_user returns count on truncation rather than an error, so an over-long name is accepted and cut with no diagnostic -- there is no ENAMETOOLONG anywhere on this path. It then calls set_task_comm(), whose __set_task_comm() in fs/exec.c copies with strscpy_pad(tsk->comm, buf, sizeof(tsk->comm)), truncating and zero-padding into the 16-byte field a second time. That second, field-level truncation is the direct analogue of ThreadName::set_name_as_bytes, which is why the fix belongs at the entry and not in the setter. Provenance, stated plainly: web access to source and man pages is blocked from this container (elixir.bootlin.com, raw.githubusercontent.com and man7.org all refused), so these function names, the count = sizeof(me->comm) - 1, and the strscpy_pad detail are from my own knowledge of the Linux tree and are NOT freshly verified against it. What IS verified first-hand is the resulting behaviour: I ran the prebuilt binary against real Linux 6.8.0-124-generic and observed the 18-byte name accepted and truncated to 'prctl05_test_xx' with a success return. The specification agrees and is quoted in the test's own header comment (prctl05.c:10-12): 'the name can be up to 16 bytes long, including the terminating null byte. If exceeds 16 bytes, the string is silently truncated.' Re-read kernel/sys.c if the fix phase has network access.
other_callers: For the defect as such, nobody else -- prctl.rs:68 is the only place in the tree where a thread name is read from user space. grep for MAX_THREAD_NAME_LEN / set_name / set_name_as_bytes / thread_name() across kernel/src finds only: the three readers (procfs comm.rs:36, stat.rs:137, status.rs:97), execve.rs:190 assigning a ThreadName built by new_from_executable_path (which already truncates via set_name_as_bytes), and clone.rs:437,575 cloning an existing ThreadName. All of those are already correct, so a narrow fix at prctl.rs:65-71 is defensible rather than merely convenient. Two adjacent facts that shape the fix without widening it: (1) Linux's other setter of the same field, write(2) to /proc/[pid]/comm, is unimplemented here -- CommFileOps::write_at (kernel/src/fs/fs_impls/procfs/pid/task/comm.rs:45-51) returns EOPNOTSUPP -- so it cannot show the bug today, but it will need identical truncating semantics when someone implements it, which is exactly why the 15-byte clamp must stay in ThreadName and not be inlined at the prctl site. (2) glibc's pthread_setname_np rejects names >= TASK_COMM_LEN with ERANGE in user space before ever issuing the syscall, so the divergence is only reachable through a direct prctl(2) call like this test's -- that is why it has gone unnoticed, and also why fixing it cannot regress any libc-mediated caller.
suggested_direction: At kernel/src/syscall/prctl.rs:65-71, replace the reject-on-overflow read with a truncating one and leave the rest of the arm alone: take a reader over the 16-byte window (CurrentUserSpace::reader is public, kernel/src/context.rs:98) and call read_cstring_until_end(MAX_THREAD_NAME_LEN) from kernel/src/util/read_cstring.rs:57, which returns Ok with a nul appended instead of None when no nul is found. Feed the result to the existing thread_name.set_name(&...) at line 70; ThreadName::set_name_as_bytes then clamps 16 to 15 and zero-fills, yielding exactly 'prctl05_test_xx'. The read must still fault: keep propagating errors so an unreadable arg2 gives EFAULT (check_vaddr_lowerbound at context.rs:273 covers the low-address case). read_cstring_until_end is already the in-tree idiom for truncating reads (procfs template/file.rs:190,209; cgroupfs; netlink link.rs:149), so this introduces no new machinery. Do not change MAX_THREAD_NAME_LEN -- 16 is TASK_COMM_LEN and is what makes the 15-byte clamp come out right -- and do not touch read_cstring or ThreadName. Expected result: prctl05 goes 8/8, matching host. Then uncomment 'prctl05' at test/initramfs/src/conformance/ltp/testcases/all.txt:1108. Out of scope but observed while reading: PR_GET_NAME at prctl.rs:72-76 writes only to_bytes_with_nul() (name length + 1) where Linux always copies the full 16-byte comm buffer; prctl05 cannot see the difference (its expected strings are 15 bytes, so both write 16, and strncmp stops at the nul either way), so leave it alone.
